_updated: 1998-07-06
- Recovery spins should start from the park side of town because that route has fewer junctions and makes it easier to maintain a genuinely easy effort (coach, 1998-07-06)
- Easy/recovery rides are to be protected even when the schedule becomes busy; relaxed breathing is the desired effort cue (coach, 1998-07-06)
- On rolling endurance rides, prefers/uses breathing and cadence cues: conversational breathing and comfortable cadence rather than surging on climbs (coach, 1998-07-06)

_updated: 1998-07-06
- For rides over two hours: target one bottle per hour and a bite of food every 30 minutes; eat a slightly larger breakfast when sustained climbing is planned (coach, 1998-07-06)
- Practice the fueling routine on easy rides before using it on longer weekend rides (coach, 1998-07-06)
- In exposed headwinds, tuck lower on the bars and move snacks earlier to stabilize energy through the final hour; monitor hand and shoulder comfort during longer low-position stints as volume increases (coach, 1998-07-06)
- On rolling terrain, hold steady endurance effort on climbs rather than surging, with conversational breathing and comfortable cadence through the middle hours (coach, 1998-07-06)

_updated: 1998-07-06
- On the second day of back-to-back rides, mild leg heaviness has cleared after about 20 minutes of easy spinning; this is currently considered a normal build-phase response requiring no adjustment (athlete, 1998-07-06)
- If second-day leg heaviness persists beyond the first 30 minutes, shorten that ride rather than pushing through (coach, 1998-07-06)
- A final riser recently felt harder than usual after a long day on the feet and into a headwind; this was attributed to situational fatigue and conditions, not declining fitness (athlete, 1998-07-06)
- Hand and shoulder comfort should be monitored when spending longer periods low on the bars, especially as weekly volume rises; no current pain or injury was reported (coach, 1998-07-06)
